💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.
  • On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system.
  • Recent findings suggest that the image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

Recent findings suggest that the image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole fresh world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an key part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

Industry observers note that the experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

According to recent reports, after a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

It has been revealed that while DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

According to recent reports, "Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m.
  • While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX introduced another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that about two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force debuts (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Industry observers note that previous classified Space Force debuts have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions released by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

Sources indicate that josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash.

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," mentioned Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

According to recent reports, his Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC remarked his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously.

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16â24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

Does football have a nitrous oxide problem?

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

Sources indicate that "It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing.".

Broughton remarked he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

Industry observers note that "I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it.".

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he stated.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', stated a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She mentioned: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up.".

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving.

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha noted more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's vital to support people who have challenges with nitrous oxide.".

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he mentioned.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide.".

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

Sources indicate that "So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died.".

If you have been affected by any of the concerns raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

#140529. Industry News: Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Industry News: Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • In a recent development, now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • Industry observers note that to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

In a recent development, now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising upcoming direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

Industry observers note that to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

Sources indicate that that resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

Sources indicate that superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Sources indicate that superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a latest class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an vital advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

Industry observers note that "We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," indicates Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

The new study provides an crucial piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," claims Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

It has been revealed that an analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

Sources indicate that in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The latest findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

According to recent reports, "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," indicates Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

It has been revealed that phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

Upcoming Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the upcoming instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.
  • The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alejandro Garnacho is yet to start a game for Aston Villa this season.

Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.

The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.

"The players who were here I think are the best players to be here with us," mentioned Emery.

Villa could have had 12 substitutes in Istanbul but Emery chose just 11 - including two goalkeepers - as Garnacho stayed at home.

The plan was for the Argentina international's loan move to become permanent for Â£43m should certain criteria be met.

They are believed to be based on a number of appearances staff felt were so achievable the club were in little doubt he would become a Villa player.

But now there is doubt he will ever play for them again.

Garnacho trained with Villa's first team on Monday but did not travel to Istanbul.

"First start after three months. Happy to be enjoying football again.".

The post Garnacho wrote on social media after a pre-season game in July has - along with anything else related to Villa - been deleted from his account.

He has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season, and seven of Villa's 11 games ended without him getting on the pitch.

His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

Including Saturday's 0-0 draw with Sunderland, Garnacho has been omitted from the past three matchday squads - a strong sign Emery has lost faith in him.

But he may have been fighting a losing battle from the off, having arrived at Villa unfit.

Sources have acknowledged the 22-year-old was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.

He initially trained on his own, and questions over the signing were already being asked, with eyebrows raised by some internally given his inconsistent form for both Chelsea and Manchester United.

Yet he had been on Villa's list of targets - albeit a long list - while he was at Stamford Bridge as Emery was keen to sign a pacy winger in the summer.

Garnacho's problems were compounded by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season, and even a boot camp during the international break in September and October, and scoring in friendlies against Sevilla and Southampton have not helped.

One of the problems Villa have is there is no exit clause, and both teams would have to agree to end the season-long loan deal early.

This time last year, Emery had already decided not to sign Harvey Elliott permanently in a Â£30m deal, leaving the on-loan Liverpool midfielder in limbo for the rest of the season.

And it appears Emery has already come to the same conclusion with Garnacho.

Industry observers note that with Villa unable to find a solution with Liverpool, Elliott wasted a precious year of his career. Those close to him recognise the damage last season did, playing just nine times after being named Player of the Tournament at the European Under-21 Championship in 2025.

He is now at Valencia and is yet to start in La Liga this season.

Sources indicate that the risk of going on loan to Villa became a topic of conversation in the game because of Elliott's plight, with sources suggesting players would think twice about joining the club. Garnacho's situation only increases those concerns.

Three times in two seasons, Emery and Villa have signed a high-profile player on loan only for it to fail.

Jadon Sancho's expensive loan from Manchester United last season - Villa paying a guaranteed 80% of Sancho's wages of more than Â£200,000 a week - ended with him having made just nine Premier League starts and scoring once in 39 appearances, with 21 of those as a substitute.

Sancho may have played more than Elliott and Garnacho - and came off the bench in their Europa League final win - but what value did Villa really get?

Of course, Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio enjoyed positive loan spells previously - Rashford returning to the England squad while at Villa - but they are exceptions to the rule.

Nicolo Zaniolo, Clement Lenglet and Axel Disasi have joined in recent years and barely merit footnotes, while Douglas Luiz's loan return last season did not prompt a return to the heights he had reached previously at Villa.

The club have constantly complained about financial restrictions with some justification, but questions can certainly be asked about the money spent on many of their signings.

The blunt truth is there is no clear path.

Teenager George Hemmings has just signed a new deal and has earned praise from Emery for understanding the way he wants his players to work.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson are also ahead of Garnacho, leaving him well behind even before regulars John McGinn, Johan Manzambi and Emi Buendia are factored in.

There was interest from abroad in the summer, with Roma keen, and it seems increasingly unlikely we will see Garnacho at another Premier League club soon.

Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the MLS - meaning Garnacho could feature for another, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.

According to recent reports, garnacho, whose character has not been called into question while at Villa, cost Chelsea Â£40m when he signed from Manchester United in 2025 but failed to make a consistent impression, with eight goals in 43 games. When he joined Chelsea he signed a contract until 2032.

Prior to that, United boss Ruben Amorim had told him to leave.

Now nothing, it seems, will persuade Emery that Garnacho is worth persevering with - leaving the winger's career continuing to drift.

  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but upcoming research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

Recent findings suggest that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Recent findings suggest that yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath upcoming deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

In a recent development, according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. Latest sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

It has been revealed that this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

It has been revealed that "Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

It has been revealed that the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some VIP Twitter owners woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk.
  • In a recent development, twitter had mentioned it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1.
  • But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the Upcoming York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some VIP Twitter owners woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

In a recent development, twitter had mentioned it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the Upcoming York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

In a recent development, william Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk indicates too bad.

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”.

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for owners over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

It has been revealed that although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

It has been revealed that in early November, Twitter rolled out the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was rapidly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual customers would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile customers. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an concern Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”.

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also noted that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laura Freigang has scored 17 goals in 45 appearances for Germany.

Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.

The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.

The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.

The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.

Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.

All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.

This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.

Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.

In a club statement, external, Franfurt stated they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".

Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.

Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel noted: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.

"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player.".

According to recent reports, furner also stated Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

The massive-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

Recent findings suggest that power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses and residential buildings: The massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under fire, affecting German companies.

According to recent reports, "Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

According to recent reports, at the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs remarked. "We are preparing for a difficult winter.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks.".

Sources indicate that energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

In a recent development, "Not a single German firm has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that military cooperation right now tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine and the software in Germany.

Industry observers note that A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," he stated.

It has been revealed that for foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act. On the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following 10 years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi stated in Berlin.

It has been revealed that "German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted. However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks.".

Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he added.

According to recent reports, at the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment.".

Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: Companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the tech giant and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different. When investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • Recent findings suggest that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Recent findings suggest that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a upcoming international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Latest Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

In a recent development, using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

In a recent development, the scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, noted:.

Recent findings suggest that "For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Sources indicate that stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer key clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

It has been revealed that "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

According to recent reports, the researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

Recent findings suggest that the international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising.
  • November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of New York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

It has been revealed that NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.

Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.

It has been revealed that this shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.

It has been revealed that our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

Sources indicate that "Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up.".

Recent findings suggest that this striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

It has been revealed that allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

"Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image.".

In a recent development, moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

Sources indicate that that Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

According to recent reports, feeling inspired to capture your own supermoon photos? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the moon and browse our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography because you don't have long to wait!

The final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

According to recent reports, so no excuses! We'd love to see your photo in our inbox next month.

#140512. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.
  • According to recent reports, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain stated on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow.
  • A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

According to recent reports, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain stated on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”.

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Industry observers note that instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

In a recent development, yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a major fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”.

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, significant mince dish.”.

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists.

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Recent findings suggest that haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

According to recent reports, from such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Industry observers note that bourdain, a native Upcoming Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:.

But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed/.

The trembling earth resounds his tread/.

Clap in his ample fist a blade/.

And legs and arms and heads will cut/.

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, stated Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

In a recent development, for Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

Best Mexican food: 23 dishes to try.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

Recent findings suggest that “From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”.

It has been revealed that its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”.

Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
